title: Generative Peptide Drug Design for AD/ADRD
text:
Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (AD and ADRD) represent a significant socio-economic burden and
a major health crisis of our time. Peptides hold promise as therapies for AD and ADRD; however, research and
discovery in the area of peptide therapeutics lag behind those of other drug classes. The proposed research
aims to empower both academic and industrial scientists to discover peptide therapeutics targeting AD and
ADRD more effectively, by creating a powerful open-source platform that integrates cutting-edge computational
and experimental technologies relevant to public health.

title: Environmental Origins of Gestational Diabetes:  PFAS-Induced Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Pancreatic Beta Cells
text:
The maternal pancreas undergoes dramatic adaptations to increase insulin production to maintain optimal
glucose levels and meet the metabolic demands of the fetus. The proposed studies will help define the role of
environmental exposure to perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) in blunting pancreatic beta cell function,
increasing insulin production, impairing mitochondrial mechanisms of ATP production, and contributing to
glucose intolerance and gestational diabetes affecting maternal and fetal health. These results will contribute
substantively to a mechanism-based understanding of PFOS’s role in pregnancy complications and alert
environmental agencies to devise policies to curtail PFOS exposure in reproductive-age women.

title: Accelerating discovery of narrow-spectrum antibiotics for Lyme disease
text:
Identification of new narrow-spectrum antibiotics could have a major impact through multiple uses in prevention
and treatment of infectious disease. We propose to develop new computational and experimental technologies
that can dramatically accelerate the narrow-spectrum drug development pipeline for Lyme disease, a major
health concern in endemic areas of the U.S. When this project is completed, we hope to contribute expandable
validated tools to rapidly screen for active compounds and identify mechanisms of drug action and novel narrow-
spectrum antibiotic candidates for Lyme disease.

title: Post-transcriptional regulation of hepatokines and systemic metabolism
text:
Relevance to Public Health
Cardiometabolic diseases, including obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease (CVD), are
leading cause of death in the United States, which therefore represents a significant burden to
the national health system. We have uncovered a novel layer of post-transcriptional regulation for
key metabolic genes, which will advance our understanding of how our body maintains systemic
metabolism and may result in improved therapeutic interventions.

title: Neuromarkers for craving and drug use
text:
This project centers on the development and validation of neuromarkers – stable indicators of biological
processes linked to pathophysiology, risk, and resilience – and in particular, the Neurobiological Craving
Signature (NCS; Koban, Wager, and Kober 2023, Nature Neuroscience), the first neuromarker validated to
predict craving and distinguish drug users from non-users across multiple studies/drug-using groups. Here we
propose to further validate the NCS on a curated dataset including 5,475 participants from 82 studies, and to
characterize its underlying neurobiological ingredients – crucial steps towards developing useful diagnostic,
predictive, and prognostic neuromarkers of substance use.

title: Systems genetics analysis of tumor evolution in the mouse
text:
Cancer is caused by exposure to carcinogenic agents that are in our environment, acting either
as chemical mutagens that directly mutate DNA, or as tumor promoters that cause chronic
inflammation and tissue damage. The effects of these exposures are modulated by inheritance
of particular cancer susceptibility genes, which together determine the outcome for individual
patients. We seek to simplify this complexity and identify underlying principles of tumor initiation,
promotion and progression using integrative systems approaches, leading to a better
understanding of human cancer complexity and novel routes to prevention or therapy.

title: Quick and Accurate Measurements of HIV Broadly Neutralizing Antibody Susceptibility
text:
PUBLIC HEALTH RELEVANCE: Early clinical trials have demonstrated the potential for bNAbs to treat and
prevent HIV infection; however, in clinical trials, participants are enrolled without knowledge of their viral
susceptibility to bNAbs, which in turn adversely affects bNAb clinical evaluation. We aim to develop
accurate assays that measure viral susceptibility to bNAbs at the point-of-care with fast turnaround so that
pre-existing and emerging resistance can be identified timely. Such information will greatly impact and
improve trials to determine the true efficacy and cutoffs for clinical use of bNAbs.

title: Structure and Dynamics of Telomeres and Telomerase
text:
The maintenance of telomeres by telomerase is necessary to support continued cell growth. Telomere and
telomerase dysfunction arise in the large majority of human cancers and certain rare genetic syndromes. This
work will signiﬁcantly advance our understanding of the molecular mechanisms governing telomere length
control and pave the way for the development of novel therapeutic interventions for human disease.

title: Washington University Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (WU-SN-TMC)
text:
Overall Project Narrative
To provide a comprehensive understanding of cellular senescence, we propose leveraging our institutional
expertise in senescence research, omics, high-resolution imaging, and informatics to establish the Washington
University Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (WU-SN-TMC) within the NIH SenNet Research Network. WU-
SN-TMC will examine dynamics and heterogeneity of senescence across four tissue types: bone marrow,
breast, colon, and liver. The knowledge gained from this undertaking will enable researchers and clinicians to
(1) more deeply understand homeostasis and (2) harness precision medicine to develop novel treatments for
age-related diseases.

title: Biobehavioral mechanisms of smartphone-based cognitive emotion regulation training for unpaid primary caregivers of persons with Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Caring for a loved one diagnosed with Alzheimer’s Disease is highly stressful. The proposed project will
investigate the biobehavioral mechanisms underlying a novel cognitive emotion regulation intervention in
unpaid primary caregivers of persons diagnosed with Alzheimer’s Disease or Alzheimer's Disease-Related
Dementias (ADRD) by examining how thinking about an emotional stimulus in a more adaptive way can predict
changes in health-related behavior via changes in negative affect and psychophysiological health-related
biomarkers. This work may hold clinical significance in the development of new interventions to improve
emotional health and well-being in caregivers of persons with ADRD.

title: Research Program: Translational and Cellular Oncology (TaCO)
text: The overarching goal of the Sidney Kimmel Cancer Center (SKCC) is to leverage research expertise to reduce the overall incidence, burden, and mortality from cancer in Greater Philadelphia and beyond. SKCC goals are realized through unique strengths in addressing cancer problems through collaboration across basic, clinical, and population research disciplines. SKCC is nucleated at Thomas Jefferson University (TJU) and enriched by fully integrated research consortium partner from Drexel University (DU); building on these strengths, SKCC focuses on addressing catchment area needs through nurturing transdisciplinary research, expanding innovative research capabilities, extending outreach and clinical research into the community, and enhancing the pace of bench-to-bedside discovery

title: Cholinergic regulation of amygdalar circuits in emotional memory
text:
Cholinergic transmission in the amygdala is critical for emotional memory as demonstrated by the
observation that deficits in this signaling underlie emotional disturbances associated with a variety of
disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, drug addiction, anxiety and trauma-related disorders, and
schizophrenia. The goal of this project is to determine at a cellular and circuit level how cholinergic
signaling modulates amygdalar circuits to regulate emotional memory. These studies will further our
understanding of the cellular and circuit mechanisms by which acetylcholine acts to regulate emotion and
inform novel avenues for the development of therapeutics to treat a variety of debilitating emotional
disorders.

title: Clinical Center for Cholestatic Liver Disease in Children
text:
We propose to remain a member of the Childhood Liver Disease Research Network (ChiLDReN) and to be a
key contributor to the strong research infrastructure that enables translational science and clinical trials in
children with biliary atresia, cholestatic syndromes, mitochondrial hepatopathies, and primary
sclerosing cholangitis. We propose to investigate the role of the TNF superfamily member TWEAK in
progression of biliary fibrosis and to determine the short-term efficacy and safety of treatment with systemic
FXR agonist in pediatric PSC. We will establish a Translational Science Coordination Center to support
ChiLDreN sites with induced pluripotent stem cell derived disease models.

title: Imaging Biomarkers of Neurotoxicity in Welders
text:
Manganese (Mn) is an established neurotoxicant that affects the same motor and cognitive brain pathways
affected in Parkinson disease (PD), notably the nigrostriatal system. In this renewal, we will use positron
emission tomography (PET) brain imaging to investigate the role of Mn in degeneration of the dopaminergic
system and the potential neuroinflammatory mechanism. Successful completion of these aims will provide a
unique opportunity to understand the mechanism of an important environmental neurotoxicant that targets the
nigrostriatal brain pathway, which is the same pathway affected in PD.

title: Developing Novel Biomarkers of Plexiform Neurofibroma Tumor Burden
text:
Currently, there are no biomarkers of tumor burden and whole body magnetic resonance imaging is expensive
and limited to few centers. We established a pipeline to identify candidate biomarker signals of tumor burden
using plasma from neurofibroma-bearing mice and generated preliminary data using samples collected in our
human NF1 repository biobank. To accomplish this, we will generate biomarker profiles from NF1 patients with
defined tumor number and location, taking advantage of the imaging and mass spectrometry laboratory used
uniquely in our clinical program.

title: Gene Therapy for Hearing and Balance Disorders
text:
DFNB1, caused by mutations in the gap junction gene GJB2, is by far the most common human hereditary
deafness, accounting for more than 50,000 cases of congenital hearing loss per year in the world. Gene addition
therapy has limited potential for long-term treatment because the AAV vector will be diluted and lost as the
GJB2-expressing cells continue to divide; instead, gene editing technologies enable long-lasting mutation
correction that restores physiologically-appropriate gene expression. Here, we seek to develop three safe and
efficient gene editing strategies for in vivo use to treat DFNB1, which together can treat up to 75% of all GJB2
mutations.

title: Decoding the role of non-coding mutations in gene regulation by cardiac transcription factors
text:
The overwhelming majority of mutations associated with congenital human disease localized to the non-coding
genome. Here, we propose an innovative approach combining high-throughput biochemical and cellular assays
to elucidate the functional outcome of non-coding mutations associated with congenital heart defects (CHD).
The success of personalized medicine depends on our understanding of mechanistic consequences of non-
coding mutations at the molecular level, in order to design and deploy the most effective preventive and
therapeutic interventions.

title: Diabetes Genomics and Analysis Core
text: DIABETES GENOMICS AND ANALYSIS CORE (DGAC): PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The SDRC Diabetes Genomics and Analysis Core (DGAC) supports the genomic research of SDRC investigators through access to next-generation sequencing and modern bioinformatics analysis. Nucleotide sequencing has become essential for formulating and resolving crucial biological questions in many contexts, like diabetes. This includes determining the underlying causes of human diseases to monitoring gene expression, elucidating regulatory networks and exploring organismal diversity that may impact human health, like human microbiomes. Researchers use this technology increasingly for an ever-broadening range of applications to detect and characterize nucleic acid molecules (RNA and DNA). The overall goal of the DGAC is to provide SDRC investigators with a next-generation sequencing facility composed of state-of-the-art laboratory, computational facilities and engaged bio-informatics support. The DGAC is committed to providing SDRC laboratories with the expertise and technical support necessary to realize the potential of next- generation sequencing in a cost-effective manner regardless of their existing expertise in genomics. This includes active evolution of core services, like the development of the wildly popular bio-informatics ‘Office Hours’ and consulting services: thus, the DGAC helps SDRC members from ‘start to finish’ with their genomics-based experiments. We will continue to offer a complete package of services ranging from study design consultation, library preparation services, access to sequencing technologies, and analysis and interpretation of sequencing data. SDRC laboratories can leverage the technologies and expertise of the DGAC to overcome cost-prohibitive barriers of entry into genomics. Based on the strengths of the DGAC and its contributions, the specific aims are to provide SDRC core users guidance with design of their next- generation sequencing projects, access to a broad range of nucleotide library preparation services, access to sequencing services with modern sequencing technologies, and support with data analysis and interpretation of their sequencing projects. The proven strengths of the DGAC in these techniques will continue to provide investigators with a unique opportunity to effectively apply powerful research approaches that would be prohibitively difficult for individual laboratories to develop. The DGAC serves as an invaluable resource for the SDRC, providing investigators with the next-generation sequencing expertise and training necessary to examine the genome at a level of access and subsidized cost for SDRC members that is not achievable at Stanford without this core. The DGAC will also serve SDRC members at UC Berkeley and UC Davis, including those supported through the proposed Regional Pilot & Feasibility Award expansion. Based on growth of the SDRC membership, evolution of exciting new technologies, and increasing membership demand for bio- informatic support and analysis, we anticipate growth in use of the specialized and unique DGAC services in the coming years.

title: Dissecting the co-occurrence of alcohol use/problems and suicidal behaviors: the roles of genetic liability and neurocognitive mechanisms
text:
Alcohol use/problems is widespread in the US and have substantial public health consequences. Alcohol
problems lead to adverse outcomes such as suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB). Preliminary evidence in
adolescents also suggests that subclinical alcohol measures are associated with STB. By combining genetics
and neuropsychology, this K99/R00 proposal offers an advanced understanding of the underlying mechanisms
involved in alcohol use/problems and STB comorbidity according to the influence of genes and environment, in
both adolescent and clinical samples.

title: Mechanisms of anti-phage defenses and their mobilization in staphylococci
text:
Staphylococci are leading causes of antibiotic-resistant infections acquired in both healthcare and community
settings. The viruses that infect these bacteria (staphylococcal phages) and the immune systems targeted
against them have profound and contrasting impacts on staphylococcal survival and pathogenic potential. The
proposed research will identify and characterize previously unknown immune systems in staphylococci as well
as mechanisms by which these and other defenses spread, thereby enabling the development of more
effective therapeutics and improved healthcare outcomes.
